Candidate 7 is a library/competitive-comparison piece about question breadth, not industry benchmark performance. No pair of candidates together holds the reusable empirical material (benchmark numbers by industry, design-choice-to-outcome linkages) that "Build from parts" would require. The asset's core value — proprietary cross-industry data mapping assessment structure to hire quality — does not exist anywhere in the current content set.

The new build is still necessary — no existing page is an interactive scoring tool, none surfaces a shareable score, and none delivers the HubSpot-Grader-style personalized output — but the question logic, scoring rubric, and report content can be assembled almost entirely from these three sources rather than researched from scratch.

Why: None of the seven pages is a salary benchmark — every candidate is a text glossary article, so the format test fails across the board. No existing page attempts the asset's defining angle: mapping actual market pay rates to demonstrated, assessed skill-proficiency levels. That said, three pages each contribute a reusable layer. The skill-based-pay page (Candidate 1) supplies the definitional spine — what skill-based pay is, its types (horizontal/vertical), and why proficiency drives compensation — that the benchmark would need as framing. The competency-based-pay page (Candidate 4) adds a calculation framework with concrete bonus-bracket examples (Communication +$2,000, Leadership +$2,500, etc.) that directly models the "pay per proficiency tier" structure the asset would display. The benchmark-job page (Candidate 3) contributes the survey-methodology scaffolding — percentile targeting, triangulating sources, compa-ratio analysis — needed to make the benchmark defensible. No single page covers topic + format + angle, but these three together provide the definitions, calculation logic, and benchmarking methodology that the new asset would build on top of.
